title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: Length of the longest contiguous slice whose characters are all distinct.
statement:
A telemetry stream repeats itself, and an operator wants the longest stretch that contains no repeated character at all.

You are given a text line. Report the length of the longest **contiguous** slice in which no character occurs twice. Characters are compared exactly as they appear: case matters, spaces and punctuation are ordinary characters, and the slice must be contiguous.

The natural technique is a sliding window plus a table of the last position each character was seen at, which lets the left edge jump forward only as far as it actually has to.
inputFormat:
The input is read from standard input as exactly one line:

1. Line 1: the text. It may contain lowercase letters, uppercase letters, digits, spaces and punctuation, but never a newline (`1 <= length <= 10^5`). Read the entire line - spaces are part of the text.
outputFormat: Print a single line containing the length of the longest slice without repeated characters as a single integer.
constraints: The line contains printable ASCII characters only (no newline inside it)
Comparison is case-sensitive and every printable character counts
notes: A slice of length 1 is always valid, so the answer is never 0. Do not compare case-insensitively and do not strip spaces: `  ` is a valid slice of length 2 and `aA` is a valid slice of length 2. A boolean 'seen' array that is never cleared is the classic wrong solution, because it must record the last index of each character rather than only whether the character ever appeared.

testCases.explanation:
Step 1: slide a window that never contains a repeated character, remembering for each character the last index at which it appeared.
Step 2: `abc` fills the window to length 3. The `a` at index 3 repeats the one at index 0, so the left edge moves to index 1 and the window becomes `bca`, still length 3.
Step 3: the same happens at every following repeat: the window becomes `cab` (length 3), then `abc` (length 3), then shrinks to `cb` (length 2) and finally to `b`.
Step 4: the longest window ever seen is 3, for example `abc` at indexes 0 to 2.

Step 1: the first `b` opens a window of length 1.
Step 2: every following `b` repeats the one immediately before it, so the left edge has to move forward each time and the window never grows.
Step 3: a single character is the best window available.
Step 4: the answer is 1.

Step 1: `pw` is a clean window of length 2.
Step 2: the second `w` repeats index 1, so the window restarts at index 2.
Step 3: `wke` then `ew` are all distinct, giving a window of length 3 ending at the final `e`.
Step 4: the answer is 3.
leading and trailing spaces are ordinary characters
upper and lower case are different characters
long run then a repeat near the end
